plan.contextChunk: This figure is a line drawing of a graphical model laid out as a two-dimensional lattice in oblique projection, built from two kinds of nodes. Open white circles occupy the lattice sites, arranged in three receding rows of three visible sites each; within a row they are joined by horizontal edges that run past the rightmost circle to the frame edge, and between rows by short diagonal edges slanting down and to the left, which likewise continue off the lower-left corner, so the grid reads as a fragment of an unbounded array. A single vertical edge rises from each white circle to a solid gray filled circle, one gray node per site, drawn above and slightly behind its partner. Only the back row carries labels: its white circles are marked with the boldface symbols x_1, x_2, and x_3, and the gray circles directly above them y_1, y_2, and y_3. Because every gray node hangs off exactly one white node while the white nodes alone form the grid, the drawing separates per-site attachments from neighbor-to-neighbor coupling. The structure depicts a Markov random field over a spatial grid, each site carrying a state variable tied to its four lattice neighbors.

elements: 3x3 grid of hidden state nodes (x) as spheres in a horizontal plane
3x3 grid of observation nodes (y) as spheres located directly above the x nodes
horizontal grid edges connecting adjacent x nodes along rows
depth grid edges connecting adjacent x nodes along columns
vertical edges linking each x node to its corresponding y node
extended horizontal edges continuing off the right side of the x-grid
extended depth edges continuing off the front-left side of the x-grid
text labels x_1, x_2, x_3 next to the back row of x nodes
text labels y_1, y_2, y_3 above the back row of y nodes

interactions.teaches: Clicking a hidden state reveals its Markov blanket: it is conditionally independent of the rest of the network given its direct lattice neighbors and its own observation node.

interactions.label: Components
interactions.teaches: Separates the neighbor coupling (grid edges representing the spatial prior) from the per-site evidence (vertical links representing the observation likelihood).

interactions.label: Coupling Strength
interactions.teaches: Increasing the pairwise potential strength forces neighboring hidden states to adopt similar values, demonstrating how the MRF encourages spatial smoothness.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Grid spans X from -1.5 to 1.5, Z from -1.5 to 1.5. Hidden nodes (x) at y=0, radius ~0.2, initially assigned varied grayscale shades (e.g., from #444444 to #FFFFFF) to represent differing initial states. Observation nodes (y) at y=1.5, radius ~0.2, solid gray #888888. Edges are thin dark lines. The 'extended' edges run an extra 0.75 units in the +X and +Z directions from the border nodes to imply an infinite lattice. Labels x_1/2/3 and y_1/2/3 are positioned near the nodes at Z = -1.5 (the back row), where X corresponds to -1.5, 0, and 1.5 respectively.
interactionPlan.notes: For nodeClick: raycast against the 9 x-nodes. On click, set opacity of the clicked x-node, its grid neighbors (distance <= 1.5), its y-node, and connecting edges to 1.0, and fade all other elements to 0.15. For modelView toggle: 'Hidden Lattice' fades out y-nodes, vertical edges, and y-labels. 'Observations' fades out the horizontal/depth grid edges. For couplingStrength slider: dynamically interpolate each x-node's initial random shade towards the global average color of all x-nodes as the slider goes 0 -> 1.

authoredContext:
To capture relationships over space, a two-dimensional (2D) structure is
useful, called a Markov random field (MRF):

Two-dimensional Markov random field.

An example of how Markov random field models are applied to images is
depicted in the figure, which show a small image region and its context
in the image (the figure [a]). The figure [b] shows an MRF with each
node corresponding to a pixel of the image region. The states of an MRF
can be indicator variables of image segment membership for each pixel.
The states of a hypothetical most-probable configuration of this MRF are
shown as the color of each node in this illustration.

Fig (a) Image to be segmented and a local region of (a) marked in red. (b) Visualization of an MRF of nodes corresponding to image pixels inside the marked region, with states indicating segment membership, for a hypothetical most probable configuration.
